title: MB7-24802
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, the appellant, a Haitian citizen, is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, the appellant, a Haitian citizen, is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). He is not submitting any evidence on appeal, but is requesting that a hearing be held. He is claiming that the RPD erred by not accepting his explanations regarding omissions in his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), by improperly assessing the evidence and by failing to analyze his counsel's submissions.

Pursuant to section 111 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination. I. BACKGROUND A. Summary of alleged facts

In his BOC Form, the appellant states that he left his country on XXXX XXXX, 2002, because he feared being murdered like his brother had been a few days prior. He also states that he entered the United States of America on XXXX XXXX, 2002, and that he applied for asylum there, but there was no follow up. On July 16, 2017, he entered Canada to obtain Canada's protection.1 Before the RPD, the appellant, then designated as the claimant, submitted a few documents as evidence.2 B. RPD decision
The hearing before the RPD was held on October 13, 2017, and the decision to reject the claim for refugee protection was rendered on November 3, 2017.
The RPD was of the opinion that the claimant's testimony lacked spontaneity because he dodged a number of questions and it contained numerous omissions that were not satisfactorily explained.3 II.

Essentially, in his memorandum, the appellant acknowledges the existence of omissions in his BOC Form, but submits that he provided reasonable explanations in that regard in his testimony before the RPD, that the RPD should have excused him for those omissions, and that it erred by not acknowledging that they were omissions regarding details and that they cannot be fatal.
paragraphs.heading_before: GROUNDS OF APPEAL AND DECISION SOUGHT

paragraphs.text: He also submits that the RPD did not adequately analyze the document from the Croix-des-Bouquets peace tribunal and that, despite the other credibility problems cited by the RPD, it was supposed to analyze it independently.
He finally submits that the RPD breached the principles of procedural fairness by not addressing and not reviewing the arguments and submissions presented to it by his counsel.

In short, the appellant requests that the RPD's determination be set aside and that he be granted refugee status or that the matter be referred to the RPD for re-determination by a different member.4 III.
In his written statement, the appellant asks for a hearing to be held before the RAD because of the RPD's errors, including its improper assessment of the evidence.5
paragraphs.heading_before: REQUEST FOR A HEARING BEFORE THE RAD

paragraphs.text: According to the case law, the onus is on the RAD to determine whether or not the criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA have been met.6 One of the determining factors is that evidence submitted as part of the appeal be found admissible. However, the appellant did not present any evidence. Therefore, because there is no new evidence to analyze as part of the appeal before the RAD,7 the request is denied.

In his memorandum, the appellant submits that the RAD must review all aspects of the RPD's decision, and that the RAD does not have to show the same deference to the RPD that that Federal Court shows to it.8
paragraphs.heading_before: IV. RAD'S ROLE AND ANALYSIS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The RAD's role is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard of review after conducting its own analysis of the record. The exception to that rule is, where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears, the RAD must then apply the reasonableness standard modified to its particular context.9 That said, the RAD's role is not to carry out a de novo consideration of the refugee claim, but rather, to determine whether, as submitted by the appellants, the RPD erred.10

Having conducted my own analysis of the record, I am of the opinion that the standard of correctness must be applied, with the understanding that deciding this case involves many elements with respect to which the RPD did not enjoy any "meaningful advantage" in terms of a first-hand observation of the appellant's demeanor.11 Having applied that standard of review, I am of the opinion that the correct decision was to reject the refugee protection claim. Here is why.

It is up to the person who is claiming refugee protection to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the facts on which they based their claim.12 The RPD and the RAD are entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, inconsistencies and omissions. Findings based on implausibility of evidence should be only made in the clearest of cases. A general finding of a lack of credibility based on these inconsistencies can extend to all relevant evidence provided by a refugee protection claimant.13 It is the entirety of the evidence that must be assessed, and members of the RPD or of the RAD may apply common sense and human experience.14

In its reasons for decision, the RPD identifies a number of omissions in the appellant's BOC Form. It took into account the explanations given in that regard, but found those explanations unreasonable. In this appeal, the appellant submits essentially that the RPD erred by not excusing him for those omissions and by considering them fatal. After carefully reviewing the RPD's decision and the appellant's arguments, I conclude that his explanations are unreasonable. Here are two examples.

First example: At the hearing, the claimant explained how he and his brother were kidnapped by a number of assailants, then brought to La Plaine, where they were told that they would make them respect the party and then they beat his brother in front of him. He also stated that, when he was about to be killed, a car passed by and the murderers fled, giving him the opportunity to escape. His explanation for omitting that incident in the BOC Form was that it was too long and that he instead summarized. Based on my own analysis, that explanation is unreasonable.

Second example: At the hearing, the claimant stated that, about a month and a half after he left his country, his assailants came to his home and beat his child and his spouse, whom they also raped. His explanation for omitting that incident in his BOC Form is that he did not want his story to be too long. Based on my own analysis, that explanation is unreasonable.

With regard to the document from the peace tribunal,15 in its reasons for decision, the RPD indicates that it analyzed it, but that it decided that, because of the refugee protection claimant's overall lack of credibility, that document alone was not sufficient to make his allegations credible. Personally, even though I find the content of that document credible, namely, that the appellant and his brother were kidnapped in 2002 and that the latter was murdered, which is clearly tragic, I am of the opinion that, at the time of the hearing before the RPD, the fear of being persecuted if he had to return and live in his country in 2017 was not established. In fact, the appellant was unable to demonstrate that, at that time, he was being sought by individuals who, in the past, wanted him for political reasons.

Because the appellant spent a number of years in the United States of America, I am of the opinion that it was reasonable to expect him to present before the RPD or before the RAD a document corroborating his allegations that, in 2017 or in 2018, he was still being sought by those individuals. But he did not do so. Failure to file supporting documents that it is reasonable to expect may have an impact on the refugee protection claimant's credibility.16 When reading rule 11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules,17 it is clear that the refugee protection claimant must provide documents and other elements supporting the refugee protection claim.

Finally, the fact that the RPD did not explicitly refer to the arguments and submissions of the claimant's counsel in its decision does not constitute, in my opinion, an error or a breach of the principles of procedural fairness.

Where procedural fairness is at issue, the proper approach is to ask whether the requirements of natural justice have been met considering the particular circumstances of the case.18 In the context of a claim for refugee protection before the RPD, procedural fairness means ensuring that the person claiming refugee protection understands the proceedings, has a reasonable opportunity to tender evidence in support of their claim, and is given a chance to persuade the RPD that their claim is well-founded.19 According to my own analysis, in this case, the RPD took into account all the evidence. Furthermore, the appellant understood the proceedings, had the opportunity to tender evidence in support of his claim and had the chance to persuade the RPD that his claim is well-founded. Consequently, the RPD complied with the principles of procedural fairness.
For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee under section 96 or a person in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
